name: Protein Folding, Molecular Chaperones, Amyloidosis and Prions

reference.source: Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry / Medical Biochemistry 5th ed
clinicalPearls: Protein folding is thermodynamically driven by hydrophobic collapse, burying nonpolar residues within the core
Molecular chaperones (Hsp70 and Hsp60 chaperonins) bind exposed hydrophobic patches to prevent aggregation
Amyloid fibrils consist of insoluble cross-beta sheet polymers displaying apple-green birefringence under polarized Congo red microscopy
Prion disease occurs when normal alpha-helical PrPC converts into protease-resistant beta-sheet rich PrPSc
Endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) polyubiquitinates misfolded proteins for 26S proteasomal destruction
reference.pathophysiology: Failure of chaperone-mediated protein folding or proteasomal clearance permits self-assembly of misfolded conformers into ordered cross-beta sheet amyloid fibrils. Fibrillar deposits resist normal tissue proteolysis, causing extracellular physical disruption and organ failure. In prion disorders, abnormal PrPSc acts as an autocatalytic conformational template, triggering progressive spongiform neurodegeneration.
additionalDifferentials: AL (primary) amyloidosis vs AA (secondary reactive) amyloidosis
Hereditary or wild-type transthyretin (ATTR) amyloid cardiomyopathy
additionalInvestigations: Tissue biopsy (abdominal fat pad, rectum, or affected organ) with Congo red staining and polarized light microscopy
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation for monoclonal light chains (AL amyloid)
Technetium pyrophosphate (99mTc-PYP) cardiac scintigraphy for transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis
CSF RT-QuIC (real-time quaking-induced conversion) assay for prion PrPSc
